stem: A dataset synced every night from an on-premises database through a Data Connection agent has not received new data for two days. The downstream transforms build successfully on schedule, but their outputs are stale. What should the data engineer check first?

choices.text: The sync's execution history together with the agent's health and the source credentials, to find whether the ingestion step itself is failing
The schedule of the downstream transforms, then force a full rebuild of every downstream dataset so that all outputs are refreshed together
The Spark details of the downstream transforms, since slow or skewed jobs are the usual reason why pipeline outputs stop reflecting new data
The permissions of the analysts who use the outputs, since stale results usually mean that consumers can no longer read the newest transactions

stem: A transform reads two reference files of a few megabytes each, joins them and writes a small lookup table every hour. Its Spark job spends most of its run time starting up, and the team wants lower cost and faster runs without changing the output. Which change fits best?

choices.text: Raise the number of Spark executors and the driver memory, since more resources let the job finish its startup phase more quickly on every run
Run the transform on a lightweight single-node compute engine, which suits small inputs and avoids most of the distributed startup overhead
Make the transform incremental, so each hourly run only processes the rows that changed in the two reference files since the previous run
Convert the transform to a streaming pipeline, so that it stays running continuously and never has to pay the job startup cost again

stem: An incremental transform normally processes a few thousand new rows per run in about two minutes. Yesterday one run took six hours and reprocessed the entire input history, although no code changed. Where should the data engineer look first?

choices.text: The executor memory settings of the transform, since a memory shortage makes incremental jobs fall back to reading the full input on every run
The downstream health checks, since a failing check forces the upstream transform to recompute its full history to repair the bad output
The build schedule, since a changed schedule makes an incremental transform run against every transaction that has accumulated in the input
The input datasets' transaction history, for a SNAPSHOT, UPDATE or DELETE transaction that made the build fall back to full computation

stem: A pipeline has five dependent datasets. Each one is scheduled to build every hour on its own timer, so builds often run when nothing upstream has changed, and the last dataset sometimes builds before its inputs finish. How should the schedule be redesigned?

choices.text: Keep separate timers but stagger them ten minutes apart, so each dataset has time to finish before the next one in the chain starts building
Replace the timers with one schedule that force-builds all five datasets every hour, so they always refresh together in a single run
Trigger the pipeline when the source updates and build the datasets in dependency order, skipping work when inputs are unchanged
Build all five datasets every fifteen minutes, so that any upstream change is picked up quickly even if some runs find nothing new

stem: An invoices dataset backs an Invoice object type. Two requirements: no invoice row with a null customer ID may ever reach the Ontology, and the team must be alerted if the dataset has not been updated for more than 26 hours. Which combination of controls meets both?

choices.text: A health check that alerts on null customer IDs, plus a build-blocking expectation that fails when the data is older than 26 hours
A filter in the transform that silently drops null customer IDs, plus a daily manual review of the dataset's last-updated time
A build-blocking expectation that rejects null customer IDs, plus a freshness health check with an alert on the published dataset
Health checks for both conditions, since a health alert prevents bad rows from reaching consumers as well as reporting stale data

stem: An analyst can see a curated dataset in a project and open its details page, but gets an access error when trying to preview its rows. Colleagues on the same team can read it. The project lead suggests making the analyst a project Owner to fix it. What should the data engineer do instead?

choices.text: Make the analyst a project Owner as suggested, since the highest project role always grants every permission that the data inside the project requires
Use Check Access to find the specific missing requirement, such as a marking or role, and request only that access through the proper approval path
Rebuild the dataset on the analyst's behalf, because access errors on a preview usually mean the latest transaction has not finished committing
Copy the dataset into a new project without restrictions and share it with the analyst, so that the analyst works on an equivalent dataset

stem: A Shipment object type uses as its primary key a row number generated in the backing transform. After a rebuild that changed the row order, users report that status edits and links now appear on the wrong shipments. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Use a stable key from the business data, such as the shipment number, or a deterministic value derived from columns that identify the shipment
Generate a new random unique ID for each row on every build, which guarantees that no two shipments can ever share the same primary key
Generate the row number after sorting by load time, so the same order is produced on every rebuild and the numbering stays the same
Use the build timestamp combined with the row number, so every key records when it was created and stays unique across rebuilds

stem: A data engineer used an AI assistant to write a new PySpark transform that joins orders to customers. The code builds successfully on a branch. Before merging, what is the most important next step?

choices.text: Merge it to the main branch first and review it afterwards, since branches only add delay when the assistant has already tested the code
Ask the assistant to rewrite the code several more times and keep the version that builds fastest, since speed is the main risk in generated code
Merge it right away, since a successful build confirms that the generated join logic and its output are correct for downstream consumers
Review it like a teammate's change: compare counts, key uniqueness and nulls with the current output and check the join's assumptions

stem: A company needs to ingest tables from an Oracle database that sits inside its corporate network with no inbound internet access, and the database team will not open the firewall. Which connection architecture fits?

choices.text: A direct connection from Foundry to the database over the internet, using the database's public endpoint and TLS for security
A nightly export from the database to CSV files that an employee uploads to Foundry by hand through the browser
A virtual table that queries the Oracle database live from Foundry, which needs no connection to be configured
An agent installed on a host inside the corporate network that makes outbound connections and runs the syncs on Foundry's behalf

stem: A transactions table with 400 million rows receives new rows continuously and existing rows are never updated. The current sync copies the whole table every night and takes seven hours. Which sync pattern should replace it?

choices.text: An append sync keyed on an increasing column such as the transaction id, fetching only rows added since the last run
A snapshot sync run twice a day, so each copy is fresher even though every run still copies the full table
An update sync that compares every row with the previous copy and writes only the rows whose values differ
A change-data-capture sync that reads the database's transaction log to replicate inserts, updates and deletes in near real time

stem: A data science team wants to explore a 2 TB table in an external cloud warehouse before deciding whether to build a pipeline on it. Copying the table into Foundry would take a day and duplicate storage. What should the data engineer offer?

choices.text: A streaming sync from the warehouse so that the data arrives continuously and the team can start exploring the first rows immediately
A virtual table that registers the warehouse table in Foundry and queries it in place, so the team can explore without first copying the data
A manual export of the table to Parquet files that the team places in a Foundry dataset using the upload feature
A snapshot sync of a 1% sample of the table, so the team can explore a small copy and then request the full copy later

stem: A sync from a REST API that ran reliably for months began failing yesterday. The agent is healthy and the credentials have not changed. The execution history shows every run ending with an error shortly after it starts. What is the most useful next check?

choices.text: Increase the sync frequency so that one of the runs succeeds between the API's intermittent failures
Replace the API connection with a new one configured from scratch, since a connection that fails after months is usually corrupted
Read the error in the sync's execution history and compare the API's current response and schema with the last successful run
Rerun the downstream pipeline with a forced snapshot build, since the error may come from stale derived datasets rather than the sync

stem: A finance team needs a curated dataset exported every night from Foundry to a partner's SFTP server. Security asks that only this one dataset can leave the platform through that route. How should it be set up?

choices.text: Configure an export to the SFTP destination under an egress policy that allows only the approved dataset through it
Give the pipeline's service user the SFTP server credentials and let the transform write the files there directly from its own code each night
Share the dataset with the partner as a Foundry user account, so they log in and download the file themselves each night
Email the file to the partner from a scheduled function, since email is already approved for external communication

stem: A customer table is ingested with an update sync keyed on a `last_modified` timestamp. Analysts notice that some customers whose addresses changed in the source still show the old address in Foundry. Which cause should be investigated first?

choices.text: The agent is too slow for the sync window, so the newest rows are cut off before the sync completes each night
The downstream Ontology object type caches old property values, so the dataset is correct but the object view is stale
The source sometimes updates the address without advancing `last_modified`, so those rows are never selected
The sync is incorrectly set to append mode, which would explain why updated rows are added rather than replaced

stem: A manufacturer wants to ingest sensor readings from 2,000 machines that publish messages to a Kafka topic at about 50,000 messages per second. Analysts need dashboards that lag the sensors by no more than a minute. Which ingestion should be set up?

choices.text: A batch sync that polls the topic every hour and writes the messages to a dataset, which is far simpler to operate than a streaming setup
A streaming sync from the Kafka topic into a streaming dataset, with a streaming pipeline aggregating for the dashboards
A virtual table over the Kafka topic so that dashboards query the live stream directly
An agent that writes the Kafka messages to CSV files and uploads them once a day

stem: A team has twenty syncs from different sources. They want to be notified when any sync fails or when a dataset has not received new data within its expected window, without checking each sync by hand. What should they configure?

choices.text: A daily manual review of the execution history of all twenty syncs by the on-call engineer
A downstream transform that fails its build whenever its input dataset is older than expected, which serves as the alert
A spreadsheet listing each sync's expected cadence, updated by whoever notices a problem
Data Health checks on the synced datasets, such as sync status and time-since-last-update, with alerts routed to the team

stem: A team of business analysts with no programming background needs to build a pipeline that joins three datasets, filters rows, derives a few columns and runs daily. Two engineers can help occasionally. Which authoring tool should the team start with?

choices.text: Code Repositories with PySpark transforms, since every pipeline eventually needs code and the analysts should learn it from the start
Contour analyses saved as datasets, since Contour is designed for analysts and can express joins and filters
Pipeline Builder, where the joins, filters and derived columns are configured visually and the pipeline is scheduled like any other
Code Workspaces notebooks, since analysts are comfortable with notebook-style exploration and can schedule the notebook as the pipeline

stem: A pipeline must parse a proprietary binary log format using a vendor's Python library, run unit tests in CI before deployment, and apply complex stateful logic. Which authoring environment fits?

choices.text: A Code Workspace notebook that runs on a schedule and imports the vendor library interactively
Code Repositories, with Python transforms that import the vendor library as a dependency and are covered by unit tests
Pipeline Builder, using built-in expressions to decode the binary format field by field
A sequence of Pipeline Builder pipelines, one per processing stage, with the binary parsing done in the first one

stem: After joining an orders dataset (1 million rows) to a customers dataset on `customer_id`, the output has 1.4 million rows. The join was meant to add the customer's name to each order. What is the correct response?

choices.text: Check whether `customer_id` is unique in the customers dataset; if it is not, fix the customer data or the join contract before rerunning the join
Filter the customers dataset to the most recent record per customer inside the join step without telling consumers, since the output count is what matters
Change the join to an inner join, since the extra rows come from orders without a matching customer that the join is padding
Deduplicate the output on the order id after the join, keeping the first row for each order, so the count returns to 1 million

stem: A dataset of support tickets contains a free-text description. The team wants a structured `category` column (one of 10 values) for every ticket, refreshed with the nightly build. Which transformation approach is appropriate?

choices.text: A Workshop app where analysts pick the category when they open a ticket, so no pipeline step is needed
A keyword lookup expression that assigns a category whenever a listed keyword appears in the description, since it is deterministic and needs no model
A manual categorization task sent to the support team each morning for the previous day's tickets
A structured LLM enrichment step that classifies each description into one of the 10 categories, with enumerated output and validation

stem: A transform aggregates 3 billion event rows per day into hourly metrics. The current single-node Python implementation runs out of memory. What should be done?

choices.text: Request a machine with more memory for the single-node engine, since the aggregation logic is simple and only the data size is the problem
Move the transform to a distributed Spark engine, which partitions the data across executors so the aggregation fits
Split the daily input into 24 hourly files and run the single-node transform 24 times, merging the results by hand
Sample 10% of the events and scale the metrics by ten, which fits in memory and is close enough for hourly reporting

stem: A transform produces a revenue column that is 30% lower than the finance team's own figure for last month. The build succeeds and the schema is correct. What should the data engineer do first?

choices.text: Rebuild the pipeline with a forced snapshot, since successful builds with wrong results usually mean stale incremental state
Ask finance to adjust their figure to match the pipeline, since the pipeline's logic has been reviewed and the build succeeded
Debug on a branch with the same inputs, comparing intermediate counts and sums with the finance definition to find the gap
Add a correction factor to the transform so that the revenue matches the finance figure, since the finance number is the source of truth

stem: A logistics dataset has delivery points as latitude and longitude, and a separate dataset of warehouse service areas as polygons. The business wants each delivery assigned to the service area that contains it. Which approach is correct?

choices.text: A manual lookup table that maps postal codes to service areas, maintained by the operations team
A nearest-warehouse calculation using the straight-line distance from each delivery to each warehouse's location
A string match between the delivery city name and the warehouse city name, since service areas follow city boundaries
A geospatial operation that performs a point-in-polygon join between the delivery coordinates and the service-area polygons

stem: A critical transform is being refactored to improve performance. The output must remain identical. How should the engineer validate the refactor before merging?

choices.text: Build the refactor on a branch against the same inputs and compare row counts, key sets and column values with the current output
Review the code carefully and merge if it reads correctly, since a performance refactor by definition does not change the logic
Merge the refactor and compare tomorrow's production output with today's; if consumers do not complain, the refactor is correct
Run the refactored transform on a 1,000-row sample and merge if the sample output matches, since any logic error would show in a sample

stem: A pipeline computes daily sales totals from an orders dataset that receives about 100,000 new rows per day and whose history is 5 years. Results are needed by 06:00 each morning. The team is considering batch, incremental or streaming. Which choice is appropriate?

choices.text: Streaming, so that the totals are always up to date and the 06:00 deadline is met by definition
Incremental processing of the new rows each night, since the input grows by appends and a nightly refresh meets the freshness need
Full batch over the entire 5-year history every night, since recomputing everything is the only way to be sure the totals are right
Lightweight single-node processing of the whole history, since daily totals are a simple aggregation

stem: A data engineer sees four transaction types in a dataset's history: SNAPSHOT, APPEND, UPDATE and DELETE. Which statement describes them correctly?

choices.text: SNAPSHOT replaces the contents entirely, APPEND adds files, UPDATE modifies or adds files while keeping the rest, DELETE removes files
SNAPSHOT is the only transaction type that can be used as an input to an incremental transform; the other three always force a full rebuild
SNAPSHOT and APPEND both add files, while UPDATE and DELETE are only used by streaming datasets and never appear in batch pipelines
APPEND replaces the dataset's contents with new files, while SNAPSHOT adds files to the existing contents

stem: A data engineer has been asked to make a transform incremental. A colleague warns that the upstream sync "sometimes rewrites the whole table". What does this mean for the incremental design?

choices.text: The incremental transform will process the snapshot as if it were new rows, doubling the output, so a deduplication step must be added
Incremental processing is impossible on this input, and the transform must stay a full batch
A SNAPSHOT upstream makes the incremental transform recompute fully for that run; tolerate it and move the sync to append where possible
The incremental transform will silently skip the snapshot runs, so nothing changes in the output and the design can ignore the warning

stem: An incremental pipeline ingests events every five minutes. After three months, downstream reads have become slow and the dataset has hundreds of thousands of tiny files. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Switch the sync to hourly, which reduces the number of files created from now on but leaves the hundreds of thousands of existing files untouched
Delete the dataset and re-ingest the three months of history in one transaction, which removes all the small files
Increase the executor count on every downstream transform so that the many files are read in parallel
Add periodic compaction that rewrites the small files into fewer, larger ones, while keeping the frequent incremental ingestion

stem: A fraud team wants alerts on suspicious card transactions within seconds of the transaction occurring. The source is a message stream. Which processing mode is required, and what should the engineer be careful about?

choices.text: Streaming, accepting the operational complexity of state, backlogs and replay because the requirement is continuous
Full batch every hour, since fraud patterns are only visible over an hour of data anyway
Incremental batch every minute, since one-minute latency is close enough and avoids the complexity of streaming
Streaming, but only for a one-week trial, after which the pipeline should be converted to a nightly batch to reduce cost

stem: A streaming pipeline that aggregates sensor readings stopped producing output two hours ago. Readings still arrive in the input stream and the pipeline reports as running. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the input stream's schema changed, since streaming pipelines generally fail silently on new fields
Whether the sensors have been reassigned to a different topic, since that would stop the input
The pipeline's backlog and lag metrics: whether it is behind the input, stuck on a failed record or blocked on state
The downstream Ontology indexing, since object views are the usual reason that streaming output appears to stop

stem: An append-only source will add two new columns next month. Several downstream incremental transforms read the dataset. How should the schema change be handled?

choices.text: Let the new columns arrive and do nothing, since incremental transforms that do not reference the columns are unaffected and those that need them can be updated when they fail
Treat it as an additive change: update the schema deliberately, verify downstream transforms on a branch against the new schema, and roll out so that consumers are not broken
Convert the incremental transforms to full batch for the month of the change, since incremental processing cannot handle any schema evolution
Create a brand-new dataset for the post-change data and ask consumers to switch, since schema changes cannot be applied to an existing dataset

stem: A team wants an incremental transform to also handle corrections: the source occasionally sends a corrected version of a record from last week. The transform currently appends everything it receives, so corrected records appear twice. What is the correct design?

choices.text: Switch the whole transform to a daily full snapshot of the source so that corrections overwrite the originals in the source before processing
Reject corrected records at ingestion, since incremental pipelines are only valid for data that never changes
Keep appending and ask consumers to take the latest record per key when they query, since the dataset should preserve every version received
Produce a current-state output by merging corrections by key, optionally alongside an append history, with a documented contract

stem: A transform that used to finish in 10 minutes now takes 90 minutes, with no code change. The input dataset has grown slightly. Which evidence should the data engineer examine to find the cause?

choices.text: The transform's code, re-reading it to find inefficient operations that were always present
The build's Spark details and a Job Comparison with the last fast build: stage durations, shuffle sizes, task skew, input files
The project's permission settings, since changed roles can slow down a build that must check access on every input file it opens
The downstream health checks, since a slow build is usually reported first by its consumers

stem: Twelve downstream datasets failed their scheduled builds overnight. Their error messages differ, but all of them read from the same curated customer dataset, which also failed. What is the correct way to handle this?

choices.text: Treat it as an upstream cascade: fix the curated customer dataset first, then rebuild the downstream datasets in order
Disable the twelve downstream schedules until each owner has reviewed their transform for defects
Rebuild all thirteen datasets immediately with force, since a transient failure is the most common reason for overnight errors
Investigate each of the twelve failures separately, since their error messages are different and may have different causes

stem: A report dataset depends on three ingestions that complete at different, unpredictable times between 01:00 and 04:00. The report must build once all three inputs for the day are present and never partially. How should the build be scheduled?

choices.text: A schedule that runs every fifteen minutes from 01:00 to 05:00, so that at least one run sees all three inputs
A time-based schedule at 04:30 every day, which is after the latest usual completion time
Three separate schedules, one triggered by each input, so the report is refreshed whenever any input arrives
An event-based schedule that waits for all three inputs to have updated since the last run and then triggers one build

stem: An engineer needs to change the logic of a production transform that feeds a dashboard used by executives. How should the change be developed and released?

choices.text: Edit the transform on the main branch during a quiet hour and watch the dashboard afterwards for problems
Copy the transform to a new dataset with a different name, point the dashboard at the copy, and delete the original later
Develop on a branch, build and validate the output there, get the change reviewed, then merge so production changes only once verified
Make the change in a notebook, run it manually to produce the new output, and upload the result over the production dataset

stem: A build fails with a message saying the executing identity cannot read one of the transform's inputs. The engineer who wrote the transform can open and preview that input. What is going on, and what should be done?

choices.text: The transform's code references the wrong dataset path, and the error message about permissions is misleading and should be ignored
The engineer's permissions have expired and must be renewed, after which the build will succeed
The build runs under a different identity that lacks access to the input; grant that identity the specific access it needs
The input dataset is corrupted and must be rebuilt by its owner before the transform can read it

stem: A monthly cost review shows that one pipeline accounts for 40% of the team's compute. Its transforms run hourly, but the consuming dashboard is refreshed once a day, and each run reprocesses the full input. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Align the schedule with the daily consumption and convert the transforms to incremental where inputs append
Move the pipeline to a lightweight engine, since lightweight compute is always cheaper regardless of data size
Keep the hourly schedule but reduce executor sizes, which lowers cost per run while preserving the current freshness
Ask the dashboard owners to refresh more often so that the hourly builds are justified by usage

stem: The team wants to catch common anti-patterns in transforms, such as unnecessary full-input scans or missing partitioning, before they reach production. Which tool supports this?

choices.text: The Ontology Manager, which validates object types but not transforms
The Linter, which analyses pipelines and flags inefficient or risky patterns that the team can address before release
Job Comparison, which compares two completed builds and therefore cannot run before the first production build
Data Health, which runs after the build and reports the resulting dataset's size

stem: A scheduled pipeline occasionally fails with an out-of-memory error on a join, roughly once a week, and succeeds when retried. The failure days correlate with a monthly bulk upload in one source. What is the smallest safe repair?

choices.text: Move the monthly bulk upload to a weekend so that the failure happens when nobody is watching the dashboard
Double the executor memory permanently, which removes the failures at the cost of higher spend on every run
Replace the join with a broadcast join, which never runs out of memory because the smaller side is simply copied to every executor in the cluster
Fix the skew on bulk-upload days by repartitioning or salting the join key, add a retry policy, and monitor memory in Spark details

stem: A data engineer is asked to explain the difference between expectations and health checks to a new team member. Which description is accurate?

choices.text: Health checks run inside the build and block it, while expectations run on a schedule afterwards and send notifications
Expectations and health checks are the same mechanism; expectations are simply health checks that are defined in transform code instead of in the user interface
Expectations apply only to Pipeline Builder pipelines and health checks only to code repositories, so the choice is made by authoring tool
Expectations run inside a build and can block the transaction when a condition fails; health checks run over time and raise alerts

stem: An Ontology object type for Patients is backed by a dataset. The patient id must be unique and non-null, and the date of birth must fall within a plausible range. Any violation must prevent the data from reaching the Ontology. What should be configured?

choices.text: Build-blocking expectations for id uniqueness, id non-null and date-of-birth range, so a violating build fails before the Ontology is updated
A Workshop validation rule that hides patients with invalid data from end users in the application while keeping the rows in the Ontology
Health checks on the dataset for null ids, duplicate ids and out-of-range dates, with alerts to the data owner
A transform that drops rows violating any of the rules, so the Ontology only ever receives valid rows

stem: A dataset's daily build succeeded, but a consumer notices that the dataset has only 3 rows today instead of the usual 2 million. Which monitoring would have caught this automatically, and what does it show about relying on build status?

choices.text: Nothing could have caught it automatically; only a consumer looking at the actual data can notice that the row count is wrong for the day
A build-status health check, which fails whenever the build produces fewer rows than the previous day
A row-count health check with a threshold, which alerts on a sudden drop; build success says nothing about completeness
The Linter, which would have flagged the transform as producing an unexpectedly small output

stem: A team wants to be warned when the distribution of a numeric column shifts (for example, the average order value doubling), but they do not want to block builds, since a shift may be a legitimate business change. Which control fits?

choices.text: No automated control, since statistical shifts are business questions rather than data engineering concerns
A health check on the column's statistics with an alert, so the team investigates shifts without stopping the pipeline
A build-blocking expectation on the column's mean, which fails the build when the mean moves beyond a tolerance
A transform that clips values to the historical range so that the average can never move much

stem: A freshness health check on a curated dataset fires every morning, but the data is actually fine and the consumers are happy. The team has started ignoring the alerts. What should be done?

choices.text: Leave it as it is, since a noisy alert is safer than no alert at all
Recalibrate the threshold to the dataset's real cadence so it alerts only on genuine lateness, and route it to owners who act
Delete the health check, since an alert that is ignored provides no value
Change the check from freshness to build status, since a build-status check only fires on real failures and never produces false alerts for the team

stem: An expectation that checks `order_total >= 0` has been failing the build for three nights because a small number of legitimate refund rows have negative totals. The dashboard has been stale for three days. What is the right resolution?

choices.text: Keep the expectation and ask the source team to stop sending refunds as negative totals
Remove the expectation entirely so that the builds succeed again and the dashboard refreshes
Change the expectation to a non-blocking warning so builds always succeed, and add a note in the dataset description telling consumers about negative values
Correct the expectation to the real rule (negatives allowed only for refund rows), fix any dashboard logic that assumed non-negatives, and rebuild

stem: A data engineer is designing monitoring for a dataset that backs a safety-critical application. Which combination gives the best coverage?

choices.text: Freshness and build-status health checks only, since those are the two failure modes that matter for an application
A single row-count expectation, since any problem in the data will show up as a change in the number of rows
Build-blocking expectations for key correctness rules, plus freshness, schema, size and status health checks with alerts to the owner
Daily manual inspection of the dataset by the application team before each release, since automated checks cannot capture safety-critical requirements

stem: A schema health check alerts that a column `customer_segment` changed type from string to integer in the curated dataset. No pipeline code changed. What should the engineer do first?

choices.text: Trace the change upstream with Data Lineage to where the type first changed, and classify it as breaking or not before altering anything
Change the downstream transforms to cast the column back to string, so consumers keep working
Rerun the build, since a type change without a code change is most likely a transient inference error
Accept the new type as an improvement, since integer segments are more efficient to store and compare than strings, and update the dataset documentation

stem: A new data engineer asks how organizations, markings and project roles combine to decide whether a user can read a dataset. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: All controls must be satisfied: the organization boundary, every marking on the data, and a project role that grants read
Markings replace project roles: once a dataset carries a marking, roles no longer matter and only marking membership is checked
Project roles override markings: an Owner of the project can read any dataset in it regardless of markings
Any one of the three is sufficient: a user who holds a project role, or who holds the right marking, or who belongs to the organization can read the dataset

stem: A team is setting up Foundry resources for a new domain: raw source syncs, cleaning transforms, curated datasets backing object types, and Workshop applications. Several other teams will consume the curated data but must not see the raw sources. How should projects be structured?

choices.text: A project per consuming team, each containing a copy of the raw sources and the curated outputs that team needs
Separate projects for sources, transforms, Ontology outputs and applications, referenced across, so each layer has its own audience
One project per dataset, so that each resource has fully independent permissions
One project for everything, with all datasets and apps together, so that lineage stays easy to follow and permissions are managed in one place

stem: A sales dataset contains rows for all regions. Regional managers must each see only their own region's rows in the same dataset-backed object type, without maintaining separate datasets per region. What should be used?

choices.text: A separate project per region containing a filtered copy of the dataset, maintained by the pipeline
A marking per region applied to the whole dataset, so only managers holding the matching regional marking can open the dataset at all
A Workshop filter that defaults to the manager's region, which they can change if they need other regions
A restricted view with a policy that filters rows by the user's region, used as the object type's backing

stem: A pipeline build fails to read a source dataset. The data engineer confirms the executing identity has the Viewer role on the datasource project. What is the most likely remaining cause, and how should it be found?

choices.text: The build is running on an old version of the transform that still points at a previous dataset; stamping a new version will fix the access error
The Viewer role is insufficient for builds; the identity must be made an Owner of the datasource project
A marking the executing identity lacks, or an organization boundary; Check Access on the dataset shows which requirement is unmet
The dataset is corrupted; it should be rebuilt by its owner

stem: A dataset containing personal data must be processed by a pipeline and then published for analysts who are not allowed to see the personal columns. What is the correct governance pattern?

choices.text: Apply the PII marking to the raw dataset only, since derived datasets are new resources whose sensitivity is decided independently of their inputs
Publish the raw dataset to analysts with the personal columns hidden by a Workshop view that does not display them
Mark the raw dataset and every derived dataset that still holds personal columns as PII, and publish an unmarked curated dataset without those columns
Give analysts the PII marking so they can read the curated dataset, since the curated dataset is what they need

stem: An application user can open a dataset-backed object type and see objects, but a particular property is always empty for them while colleagues see values. The pipeline and dataset are healthy. What should the data engineer check?

choices.text: Whether the object type needs to be re-indexed, since indexing lag shows up as missing property values
Whether a column- or row-level policy on the backing dataset or restricted view hides that column for this user, via Check Access
Whether the user's browser is caching an older version of the application module, since empty properties are usually a display problem on the client side
Whether the pipeline dropped the column for some rows, since a healthy build can still produce nulls

stem: An engineer needs to debug a transform that reads a marked dataset, but holds neither the marking nor access to the datasource project. The engineer proposes to export the data to a personal folder to work on it. What should happen instead?

choices.text: Approve the export to the personal folder, since the engineer genuinely needs the data to fix the bug and a personal folder is private to its owner
Remove the marking temporarily for the duration of the debugging and restore it afterwards
Ask a colleague who holds the marking to copy the dataset into an unmarked project for the engineer
Request the marking through its approval process, or debug with a reviewed de-identified sample, keeping the data governed

stem: After introducing a restricted view to filter rows by region, a downstream transform that reads the view returns far fewer rows than expected when it runs, and a different count when a developer previews it. What explains this?

choices.text: Restricted views filter by the reading identity, so the build identity and the developer see different rows; the transform should read the right source
The transform's cache is stale; clearing the developer's preview cache will align the counts
The restricted view is corrupted and must be recreated before the transform can read all rows
Restricted views always return a random sample of the rows to protect privacy, which is why the counts vary from one read to the next

stem: A curated dataset has one row per order line with columns for the order, the customer, the product and the quantity. The business wants to ask questions such as "which customers bought this product" and "what did this order contain". How should this be modeled in the Ontology?

choices.text: One object type Customer with a list property containing every product the customer ever bought
Object types Customer and Product only, with the quantity stored as a property on a link between them
One object type OrderLine with all the columns as properties, since the dataset already has the shape that the business questions need
Object types Order, Customer, Product and OrderLine, with links from OrderLine to Order and Product and from Order to Customer

stem: An Employee object type is being created from an HR dataset. The candidates for primary key are the email address, the employee number assigned by HR, and the row's position in the dataset. Which should be the primary key?

choices.text: The row position, since it is guaranteed unique within any dataset and requires no business knowledge
A new UUID generated on each build, since UUIDs are globally unique by construction
The employee number, since it is assigned once, never changes, and is unique for each person
The email address, since it is human-readable and unique in the company directory

stem: A link type between Shipment and Carrier is configured as one-to-one. Operations report that some shipments show no carrier even though the dataset has carrier assignments, and that a carrier's shipment list only ever shows one shipment. What is wrong?

choices.text: The cardinality is wrong: a carrier handles many shipments, so the link must be many-to-one from Shipment to Carrier
The dataset's carrier column has nulls that must be filled before the link can be created
Link types cannot connect object types that are backed by different datasets, so a join dataset combining shipments and carriers must be created first
The link type is backed by the wrong dataset and needs to be re-pointed to the shipments dataset

stem: A dashboard team asks for an object type "SalesSummary" with properties such as total revenue this month, top product, and number of open tickets per region, so that their dashboard can read everything from one object. What should the data engineer recommend?

choices.text: Create SalesSummary as requested, since object types should be shaped around how the consuming applications need to display the data
Model the entities (Sale, Product, Ticket, Region) and let the dashboard aggregate over links or a derived aggregate dataset
Create one SalesSummary object per region per month so that the dashboard can filter it by both dimensions
Create SalesSummary but rename it to make it clear that it is for the dashboard only

stem: A live object type used by three production applications needs a new property and a renamed link type. The team must not disrupt the applications while developing the change. How should this be done?

choices.text: Freeze the applications for a day while the changes are made and tested on the live object type
Use Global Branching to develop the changes on a branch, validate them with the applications there, and merge once they pass
Create a copy of the object type with the new structure, migrate the applications to the copy one by one, and delete the original
Make the changes directly on the live object type during off-hours, since Ontology edits apply instantly

stem: Applications need each Customer's "lifetime value" (sum of all order totals). It is needed by dashboards, filters and an AI workflow, and it only needs to be refreshed daily. Where should it be computed?

choices.text: In the AI workflow, which can compute it on demand and share the result with the dashboards
In every application separately, so each team controls its own definition
North of the Ontology, in a function that sums orders over links each time an application displays a customer
South of the Ontology, in the pipeline that builds the Customer dataset, exposed as a property

stem: Several object types (Truck, Forklift, Crane) share properties like asset id, location and maintenance status, and applications want to show "all assets needing maintenance" regardless of type. Which Ontology feature fits?

choices.text: Define an Asset interface with shared properties implemented by all three types, so applications query the interface
Create a fourth object type AssetSummary that copies the shared properties from the three types each night
Add links from each type to a central Asset object that holds the shared properties, keeping them in two places that the pipeline updates nightly
Merge the three object types into one Asset type with a type column, dropping the type-specific properties

stem: A product team wants to change the primary key of a live Order object type from an internal row id to the business order number. Users have made edits and created links on the existing objects. What must the data engineer plan for?

choices.text: Keeping both keys as primary keys so that old and new references continue to work side by side
Deleting all existing edits and links, since they belong to the old key and cannot be preserved in any way
A migration: map old keys to new keys, migrate existing edits and links, update consumers that reference the old key, validated on a branch
Nothing special; changing the primary key in the object type configuration remaps all the existing edits and links to the new key automatically

stem: A data engineer wants to understand which AI capability to use for each of three needs: getting help writing a PySpark transform in the code editor, asking how a platform feature works, and adding a column that summarizes a free-text field for every row of a dataset. Which mapping is correct?

choices.text: AIP Assist for all three, since it is the platform's general assistant
A data-producing LLM transform for all three, since every need involves a language model
A code assistant for writing the transform, AIP Assist for the platform question, and an LLM transform for the per-row column
An LLM transform for writing the transform code, AIP Assist for producing the summary column, and a code assistant for the platform question

stem: An LLM transform extracts a structured "incident type" from maintenance logs. The team wants the results to be reliable enough to back an Ontology property. Which configuration is appropriate?

choices.text: Enumerated structured output, code validation of the value, caching by input text, and a quality check flagging invalid results
A prompt instruction asking the model to be accurate, with the output written to the column as is
A second model call that rewrites the first model's free-text answer into one of the allowed types
Free-text output from the model written directly to the column, since the model's own wording is more informative than any fixed list of types

stem: Two requests arrive: (1) tag every one of 3 million documents with a topic, used by filters in several apps and refreshed weekly; (2) let an analyst ask free-form questions about one document while reading it. Where should the AI processing for each run?

choices.text: Both in the pipeline: tag the documents weekly and also pre-generate answers to a list of likely questions for each document in the same run
Both at the application layer: tag documents when a user opens them and answer questions on demand
Tagging at the application layer and questions in the pipeline, since questions are more predictable than tags
Tagging as a batch LLM transform in the pipeline; free-form questions answered interactively at the application layer with the document as context

stem: A code assistant generated a transform that reads a large dataset, collects it to the driver, and loops over rows in Python to compute a running total. The build succeeds on a sample but fails with out-of-memory on the full input. What should the engineer conclude?

choices.text: The dataset is too large for Foundry and should be sampled permanently
The generated code collects a distributed dataset to one node, an unsupported pattern at this size; rewrite it with distributed operations
The sample build already proves the logic is correct; the full build should simply be retried with more executors until it passes
The assistant's code is correct and the cluster needs more driver memory

stem: A pipeline enriches 5 million customer reviews with an LLM-generated sentiment score. The prompt is being improved every week, and the team wants to avoid reprocessing every review on each change while still updating old results eventually. Which design is appropriate?

choices.text: Reprocess all 5 million reviews whenever the prompt changes, since consistency requires every row to have been scored with the same prompt
Reprocess only reviews from the last week, since older reviews are rarely viewed
Never reprocess old reviews, since the sentiment of a review does not change
Cache results by review text and prompt version; process new reviews with the current prompt and backfill older ones gradually

stem: A data engineer is asked to add embeddings for product descriptions so that a semantic search over products can be built. Where does this work belong?

choices.text: In the pipeline, as an embedding transform writing a vector column, exposed as a vector property on the Product object type
In a notebook run once by hand and uploaded as a dataset, since embeddings only need to be created once
In the application, computing embeddings for the products when a user searches, so that the vectors are always current at query time
In an agent that embeds products during conversations and stores the vectors in its memory

stem: An AI assistant suggested replacing a transform's inner join with a left join "to avoid losing rows". The engineer applied it, the build passed, and the row count rose by 3%. Downstream, a revenue dashboard now shows null customer segments for some orders. How should this have been handled?

choices.text: Keep the change, since more rows is better and the dashboard team can filter out nulls
Review the suggestion against the data contract first: the join type changes semantics; validate on a branch and check consumers, then decide
Apply the left join but add a filter that removes rows with null segments, which restores the previous count
Revert to the inner join and ask the assistant for a different suggestion, since assistants should never propose changes to join types in production transforms

stem: An LLM transform classifies 100,000 documents nightly. The team notices the invalid-output rate jumped from 1% to 9% last night with no prompt change. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Lower the validation strictness so that more of the outputs pass, which returns the invalid rate to its normal level without touching the pipeline
Rerun the transform with a higher temperature to get more varied outputs that may fit the categories
Treat it as a quality incident: sample the invalid outputs, compare model and prompt versions and inputs with the previous night, and hold affected rows
Nothing, since the pipeline still succeeded and 9% is a small fraction of the documents

stem: A team needs to ingest files that a partner drops onto an SFTP server every night, each file named with the date. Which sync configuration fits?

choices.text: A streaming sync that watches the SFTP server for changes and emits each line as a message in real time
A file-based sync on an SFTP source that picks up new files matching the naming pattern and appends them to the raw dataset
A manual download of each file by the on-call engineer every morning, followed by an upload through the browser into the raw dataset
A JDBC sync pointed at the SFTP host, since all network sources are reached through the same database driver

stem: A CDC sync replicates a customer table including deletes. Analysts report that customers deleted in the source still appear in a downstream curated dataset. Where is the problem likely to be?

choices.text: In the agent, which drops delete events when the network is slow
In the CDC sync, which by design captures only inserts and updates and never deletes, so the source team must stop deleting rows entirely
In the Ontology, which caches deleted objects for 30 days before removing them
In the downstream transform, which treats the change records as appends and never applies the delete markers to its output

stem: A data engineer notices that a sync's source credentials are written in a transform's code so that the transform can query the source directly as well. What should be done?

choices.text: Nothing, since credentials in code are acceptable when the repository is private
Move the credentials into the dataset's description so they are easier to find
Remove them from the code; keep them in the Data Connection source configuration and have the transform read the synced dataset instead
Encrypt the credentials inside the code with a symmetric key that is also stored in the same repository, so they are no longer readable in plain text

stem: An agent-based sync has started failing intermittently: some runs succeed, others fail with connection timeouts to the source. The agent host is shared with other software. What is the right investigation?

choices.text: Correlate failure times with the agent's health and host resource usage, the source database's load, and network stability
Reinstall the agent on the same host, since intermittent failures of this kind usually mean the installation has become corrupted over time
Increase the sync frequency so that successful runs outnumber failures
Switch to a direct connection, which does not need an agent and therefore cannot time out

stem: A source table has 2 million rows, no reliable timestamp or increasing key, and about 5% of rows change each day in place. Which sync pattern should be used?

choices.text: A streaming sync, since in-place changes are best captured continuously
An update sync on a `last_modified` column that the source does not have
A daily snapshot sync, since without a change signal there is no safe way to identify changed rows, and the copy is affordable
An append sync keyed on the primary key, which will capture the changed rows automatically because their keys already exist in the dataset

stem: Analysts want to run ad hoc SQL against a large external data warehouse table from Foundry, but the warehouse team forbids copying the data out. Which approach respects the constraint?

choices.text: An agent that caches the table on its host so analysts can query the cache
Exporting the table to CSV and emailing it to analysts
A snapshot sync run once at night into Foundry, since a nightly copy for analytics is not really "copying the data out" of the warehouse
A virtual table registered over the warehouse table, so queries are pushed to the warehouse and the data stays there

stem: A newly configured REST API sync returns only the first 1,000 records on every run although the source has 80,000. What is the most likely configuration problem?

choices.text: The API requires a streaming sync to return more than one page
Pagination is not configured, so the sync reads only the first page of the response and never requests the next pages
The dataset's schema has a 1,000-row limit set in the Ontology
The agent's memory limit on its host, which caps the number of records a single sync run can hold before writing them to the dataset

stem: A company must ingest data from 40 similar on-premises sites, each with its own database behind its own firewall. Which connection architecture scales best while keeping each site's network closed to inbound traffic?

choices.text: An agent at each site connecting outbound and running that site's syncs, managed centrally with health monitoring and standard configuration
One central agent in the head office that opens VPN tunnels into each site
Direct connections from Foundry to each of the 40 site databases after every site's firewall has been opened for inbound traffic from the platform
A nightly email from each site containing a database dump

stem: Three regional sales datasets have the same columns but different column orders and one region uses a different name for the amount column. The team wants one combined dataset. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Copying all three into a spreadsheet and pasting them together before uploading
Three separate outputs kept as they are, since datasets with different column orders and names cannot be combined safely into one dataset
A join of the three datasets on the sales id, which brings all the rows into one output
A union after aligning schemas: rename the odd column, select columns in one order with consistent types, and add a region column

stem: A transform needs a Python library for a specialized statistical computation that has no Spark equivalent, on an input of about 500 MB that fits in memory. Which engine and approach fit?

choices.text: A lightweight single-node Python transform that imports the library and processes the dataframe in memory, since the data fits
Rewriting the statistical computation in SQL so that no library is needed
Spark with the library called inside a user-defined function on every executor, which is the only way to use Python libraries in a Foundry transform
Running the library in a notebook by hand each week and uploading the result

stem: A transform computes a monthly rollup. For February the output has 31 days of data, including three days that belong to March. What is the right debugging approach?

choices.text: Delete the three March rows from the February output by hand using a dataset edit so that the monthly rollup looks right for the report
Reproduce on a branch, inspect the date logic (time zone, inclusive end), fix it, add a test and a date-range expectation, rebuild
Ask consumers to filter the extra rows themselves since the data is otherwise correct
Change the rollup to cover six weeks so that the boundary never matters

stem: A team must compute, for each customer, the number of orders in the last 90 days, the total value, and the date of the most recent order, refreshed daily for an Ontology property set. Which transformation pattern is correct?

choices.text: A row-level expression on the orders dataset that writes the customer's count, total and latest date onto every one of that customer's order rows
A join of orders to customers without aggregation, leaving the counting to the application
An aggregation by customer over orders from the last 90 days giving count, sum and max date, joined to the customer dataset
A manual pivot table built by an analyst every morning and uploaded as the customer dataset

stem: A Pipeline Builder pipeline has grown to 60 nodes with repeated logic in several branches, and the team struggles to review changes. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Rewrite the entire pipeline in code transforms immediately, since visual pipelines cannot be maintained once they pass a few dozen nodes
Keep adding nodes, since Pipeline Builder is designed for pipelines of any size
Refactor: extract shared logic, split into stages with intermediate datasets, and move complex branches to tested code transforms where useful
Freeze the pipeline and forbid further changes to avoid breaking it

stem: A transform deduplicates customer records by email address. Reviewers find that two different customers who share a family email were merged into one. What should change?

choices.text: Stop deduplicating entirely so that no customer can be lost
Revise the key: use the business identity (customer id, or name plus date of birth plus email) and route ambiguous matches to review
Deduplicate by name instead of email
Nothing, since customers who share an email address are rare and merging a few of them is an acceptable loss for a cleaner dataset

stem: A code transform has a function that normalizes phone numbers into an international format. Which testing approach is appropriate?

choices.text: Unit tests for typical, edge (missing country code, extensions, empty) and bad inputs in CI, plus an output-format expectation
No tests, since the function is small and obviously correct
A test that only checks that the transform builds without error
Manual spot checks of a few dozen rows in a preview of the output dataset after each build, done by whoever is on call that day

stem: A dataset of 10 million product images must be processed to produce a thumbnail and the image dimensions for each. Which transformation approach is appropriate?

choices.text: A row-level expression in Pipeline Builder that reads each image's bytes as a string column and extracts the dimensions from the header text
A manual batch where an analyst opens each image and records its size
An LLM transform that describes each image in words
A media processing step over the image files producing thumbnails and a dimensions dataset, run as a distributed batch

stem: A dashboard needs hourly refresh of metrics computed over a 10 TB event history that grows by 50 GB a day. Which processing mode keeps cost reasonable while meeting the hourly need?

choices.text: Streaming, since the only way to refresh hourly is to process events as they arrive
Full batch every hour, recomputing the entire 10 TB history on each run, since the dashboard must be refreshed hourly and batch is simplest
Incremental processing of each hour's new events into running aggregates, with a periodic full recompute to reconcile
Daily batch, telling the business that hourly refresh is not possible at this scale

stem: A transform's output dataset shows a history of UPDATE transactions rather than APPEND, although the transform is meant to add new daily files. Downstream incremental transforms are falling back to full recompute every day. What should be checked?

choices.text: Whether the schedule runs too often, since frequent runs generate UPDATE transactions
Whether the dataset's schema has changed, since schema changes always produce UPDATE transactions
Whether the downstream transforms have enough executor memory, since a fallback to full recompute is usually caused by a resource shortage
How the transform writes its output: UPDATE (replacing files) instead of APPEND; change it to write new files only

stem: A streaming pipeline failed for three hours overnight and the input stream retained the messages. After the fix, how should the gap be handled?

choices.text: Replay the retained messages from the last processed offset, with idempotent processing so twice-processed messages do not duplicate
Restart the pipeline from the latest message and backfill the three-hour gap manually from a spreadsheet exported by the source team
Convert the pipeline to batch to avoid gaps in future
Ignore the three hours, since streaming data is only valuable in real time

stem: Which description correctly pairs a requirement with the appropriate processing mode?

choices.text: Nightly report on yesterday's sales: streaming; alert within seconds on a sensor threshold: nightly batch; small lookup table: full Spark batch
Nightly sales report: batch or incremental; seconds-level sensor alert: streaming; small daily lookup from two 5 MB files: lightweight
Every requirement: full batch, since it is the simplest mode
Every requirement: streaming, since it is the most capable mode

stem: An incremental transform maintains a running total per account. After an upstream correction was delivered as an UPDATE transaction, the totals for some accounts are now wrong even though the transform ran successfully. Why, and what should be done?

choices.text: The UPDATE should have been rejected by a build-blocking expectation on the input; add one now and ignore the totals that are already wrong
Running totals cannot be computed incrementally; switch to daily full batch forever
The fallback recompute was combined with the old running-total state, double counting; make state fallback-aware and recompute the totals
The transform is bugged in its arithmetic; rewrite the sum logic

stem: A data engineer wants to confirm, before enabling an incremental transform in production, that it produces the same result as the full batch version. Which validation is appropriate?

choices.text: Enable the incremental version in production now and compare its results with a batch run in a month, when there is enough history to judge
Run the incremental version once and check that it finishes faster
Trust the incremental logic, since the code was reviewed
Run batch and incremental versions on a branch over the same inputs across several runs, including one after an upstream UPDATE, and compare

stem: A dataset's transaction history shows: SNAPSHOT (Monday), APPEND (Tuesday), APPEND (Wednesday), DELETE (Thursday, removing Tuesday's file). What is the dataset's current view?

choices.text: Monday's files plus Wednesday's file; Tuesday's file was removed by the DELETE
Nothing, since a DELETE transaction empties the dataset
Only Wednesday's file, since the latest transaction defines the view
All files from Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, since DELETE only marks files as hidden

stem: A streaming pipeline's state (per-key windows) has grown to the point that the job restarts often with memory errors, and the key space keeps growing. What should the data engineer change?

choices.text: Convert the pipeline to batch and give up on streaming
Bound the state with windows and time-to-live so inactive keys are evicted, and move long-horizon aggregates to batch over the persisted stream
Give the job unlimited memory on a larger machine, since per-key state must be kept for every key forever to keep the windows correct
Reduce the input rate by sampling messages

stem: A dataset consumer reports that a value changed unexpectedly between yesterday and today. The data engineer wants to find which transform in a twelve-step pipeline introduced the change. Which tool and approach are right?

choices.text: Compare the two builds' Spark details for all twelve transforms and treat whichever transform ran noticeably longer today as the one that changed the value
Walk upstream with Data Lineage, comparing the key's value in each intermediate dataset across the two builds, to the first stage that differs
Rebuild the entire twelve-step pipeline from the top with force and check whether the value changes back to yesterday's figure
Ask every transform owner to check their code for bugs

stem: A pipeline must run once a day but must not start before 03:00, and must also wait for its input to be updated that day. How should the schedule be expressed?

choices.text: A time trigger every hour from 03:00 that force-builds regardless of the input
Two independent schedules on the same dataset, one firing at 03:00 and one firing on each input update, so whichever condition is met first builds
One schedule combining both conditions: triggered by the input update, with the build not starting before 03:00
A time trigger at 03:00 only, assuming the input is always updated by then

stem: A build fails with a Spark error indicating a single task failed repeatedly with a serialization exception on a particular input file. Other tasks succeed. What classification and action are appropriate?

choices.text: A data problem in one input file; inspect it, quarantine or correct it at the source, and add validation so a bad file fails clearly
Upstream cascade; rebuild the upstream dataset
Resource limit; add more executors
Permission failure on that file; grant the build identity broader access to the input dataset's project so every task can read every file

stem: Two engineers are working on different changes to the same pipeline. One change is urgent; the other is a large refactor that will take weeks. How should branches and releases be managed?

choices.text: The refactor is paused until the urgent fix is finished and released, after which both engineers work on the main branch one after the other
Both edit the main branch, coordinating by chat to avoid conflicts
The urgent fix is applied directly in production and the refactor branch ignores it
Separate branches; the urgent fix is validated, reviewed and merged first; the refactor branch stays synchronized with main and merges when complete

stem: After an incident, the team wants to prevent a repeat of a pipeline that silently processed an empty input. Which operational safeguards should be added?

choices.text: An email to the team asking everyone to be more careful
Doubling the schedule frequency so that if an empty input is processed, the next build picks up the real data twice as quickly
A build-blocking minimum-row-count expectation on the input, a Data Health size check with an alert to the owner, and a runbook entry
A nightly manual check of input sizes by the on-call engineer

stem: A pipeline that was fast became slow after the team added a new column computed by a Python UDF applied to every row of a 2 billion row dataset. Spark details show that stage dominating. What is the appropriate fix?

choices.text: Move the UDF to run on the driver node after collecting the dataset, since the driver typically has more memory than any single executor
Accept the slowdown, since the column is required
Double the executor count to run the UDF faster
Replace the row-wise Python UDF with native dataframe functions or a vectorized UDF so the computation stays inside the engine

stem: A team asks for every dataset in their project to build every 10 minutes "so that nothing is ever stale". What should the data engineer recommend?

choices.text: Build every 10 minutes but only on weekdays
Schedule each dataset by its source cadence and consumer needs, with event-based triggers where inputs update unpredictably
Build everything once a week to minimize cost
Agree to the request, since more frequent builds can only improve freshness and compute cost is a secondary concern compared with stale data

stem: A pipeline change is ready on a branch and validated. The release will change a column's semantics that two downstream teams depend on. How should the release be executed?

choices.text: Announce the change with a date, provide a transition period with both columns, merge at the agreed time, monitor downstream, keep rollback
Merge at night when nobody is watching to reduce complaints
Never change column semantics; create a new pipeline instead
Merge immediately, since the branch is validated; the two downstream teams will notice the change in their next builds and adapt their logic

stem: An orders dataset must satisfy: order id unique, customer id present, amount non-negative except for refunds, and order date not in the future. A build that violates any rule must not publish. Which expectations should be defined?

choices.text: A single expectation that the dataset "looks correct" evaluated by a reviewer each morning
Health checks for each rule, since health checks are easier to configure than expectations
One expectation that the row count is above zero on every build, since any real data problem in the source will reduce the number of rows delivered
Separate build-blocking expectations: order id unique, customer id not null, amount rule conditional on order type, order date not in the future

stem: A dataset's freshness check has not fired, yet the data is stale: the last transaction is three days old. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: The dataset is too small for health checks to apply
Freshness checks cannot detect staleness longer than 24 hours
The check is misconfigured or not running (window too wide, wrong dataset or branch, failed execution, broken routing); verify and correct it
Freshness checks only alert when a scheduled build fails with an error, not when no build runs at all, so a silently skipped schedule is invisible to them

stem: A pipeline publishes a dataset used by both an Ontology object type (where correctness is critical) and an exploratory analytics team (who tolerate imperfections). A new rule would block builds on any null in a secondary column. What is the right approach?

choices.text: Decide by consequence: block only if the null breaks the critical consumer; otherwise monitor it and handle nulls in the Ontology's backing transform
Remove all expectations so the analytics team never waits for data
Block on the rule for everyone, since stricter is always safer
Create two completely separate pipelines from the same source, each with its own rules, one for the Ontology and one for the analytics team

stem: A team wants to detect when the distinct count of `country` in a dataset suddenly drops (for example from 40 to 3), which has happened once due to a broken join. Which health check should they configure?

choices.text: A build-status check, since a broken join fails the build
A content check on the distinct count of `country` with an alert when it falls below a threshold or deviates from history
A schema check on the dataset, since a broken join usually changes the column types or drops the country column from the output entirely
A freshness check, since a broken join delays the build

stem: An expectation on a large dataset adds 20 minutes to each build because it checks uniqueness over 3 billion rows. The team wants to keep the protection but reduce the cost. What are reasonable options?

choices.text: Remove the expectation, since 20 minutes is too expensive for a check
Keep the guarantee but make it cheaper: incremental slice check plus an anti-join on existing keys, a less frequent full check, or an upstream guarantee
Convert it to a health check that runs after publishing, accepting that duplicate keys may reach the Ontology and its consumers for a while before anyone reacts
Check uniqueness on a 1% sample, which is representative

stem: Alerts from health checks across 200 datasets go to one shared channel, and the team is overwhelmed. What should be changed?

choices.text: Turn off the alerts, since nobody can read them anyway
Send all alerts by email instead of chat
Keep the single shared channel but ask the whole team to check it more often and to acknowledge each alert with a reaction so nothing is missed
Route by ownership and severity: critical datasets page on-call, others go to the owning team, with deduplication and context

stem: Which statement about expectations and incremental transforms is correct?

choices.text: Expectations apply to incremental transforms; slice-level checks run on new rows, while global checks like uniqueness need a full or incremental-aware strategy
Expectations cannot be used on incremental transforms at all, since every check would need to scan the entire dataset history on every single run
Expectations automatically convert an incremental transform into a full batch transform
Expectations on incremental transforms only run during fallback snapshot builds

stem: A health check on a dataset's row count has been failing for a week because the dataset legitimately shrank after a business change. The team has been ignoring it. What should happen?

choices.text: Nothing for now; the check's anomaly baseline will eventually adjust itself to the new dataset size as more builds accumulate at the smaller volume
Delete the check permanently
Re-baseline the check to the new expected size and record the business change, because an ignored failing check hides any future real problem
Double the dataset artificially so the check passes
